home.heroTitle: Cross-chain security across the software lifecycle
home.heroBody: The cross-chain Secure SDLC is a closed lifecycle of five phases; the three thesis studies secure the design phase, pre-deployment coding and auditing, and post-deployment operations and optimization.
home.sdlcBody: Each study is a self-contained module with its own page; there is no end-to-end pipeline coupling them.

chain.title: Real Solidity contracts
chain.body: Two in-memory EVM chains (py-evm): chain-A (id 31337) and chain-B (id 97). Every transaction is mined into its own block for easy observation.

ml.title: Compact algorithms, instant feedback
ml.body: ZKP, threshold signatures, CP-ABE and numpy/scikit-learn ML with fixed seeds — every action responds in under 3 seconds.

cd1.name: Π_univ
cd1.summary: Cross-chain academic credentials: the source chain anchors a Merkle commitment, the holder proves a business predicate in zero knowledge, a relay committee co-signs t-of-n and the destination chain verifies with ecrecover.
steps: Setup & key generation
Issue credential
Generate ZK proof
Cross-chain verification
Revocation

sw.title: Statement vs Witness
sw.statementHint: Relays and the destination chain only see this.
sw.witnessHint: Never leaves the holder's device; only used to build the proof.
sw.unsat: predicate not satisfied → proof will fail

tamper.title: Tampering lab
tamper.body: Each button re-runs verification under an attack; the chain-B contract itself rejects it via ecrecover, threshold and nonce.

shamir.title: Shamir (t, n) — nobody holds the whole key
shamir.body: Secret 1234 is split into 5 shares with a degree t−1 = 2 polynomial. Pick shares: with 3 shares Lagrange interpolation at x = 0 gives the secret; with 2 it fails.

tour.s0: Reset the session: two fresh EVM chains — chain-A (university) and chain-B (employer).
tour.s1: Setup: deploy CredentialRegistry on chain-A and ThresholdVerifier with 5 relays and threshold t = 3 on chain-B.
tour.s2: The university issues 5 credentials: each is a commitment (hash + Pedersen); only the Merkle root is anchored on chain-A.
tour.s3: Student S3 proves “GPA ≥ 3.2” in zero knowledge — the statement is public, GPA and randomness stay on the device.
tour.s4: Relays independently check Merkle, revocation and ZKP, then sign; the gateway submits the fastest 3/5 → chain-B verifies with ecrecover and accepts.
tour.s5: The attestation record is CP-ABE encrypted: only ACME's HR or an Auditor can decrypt it.
tour.s6: Tamper: only 2 relays sign (below threshold) → the contract emits AttestationRejected.
tour.s7: Tamper: signatures from keys outside the committee → ecrecover yields unknown addresses, 0 valid signatures.
tour.s8: Replay an already accepted message → the transaction reverts “replay: already accepted”.
tour.s9: The university revokes S3's credential on chain-A.
tour.s10: S3 proves again: relays read the revocation on chain-A and refuse to sign → chain-B rejects.
tour.s11: Summary: the destination chain decides on cryptographic evidence, not on relay reputation.

cd2.name: CrossGuard
cd2.topic: Vulnerability detection and auditing of cross-chain smart contracts
cd2.summary: Pre-deployment audit of bridge contracts: multi-source representation, few-shot classification, differentially private federated training and an audit report with protocol invariants.
steps: M1 · Multi-source representation
M2 · Few-shot detection core
M3 · DP-SGD federated training
M4 · Audit report
Exploit lab

desc.ex: Demonstrate impact on a real EVM

m3.note: 5 clients · softmax regression · DP-SGD (clip C, Gaussian noise) · moments-accountant ε · averaged over 4 seeds.

ex.pickVuln: Pick a vulnerable contract to run an attack.
ex.blocked: The fix blocks the attack — transaction reverted

tour.s0: Pick VulnBridgeNoNonce — a bridge that mints tokens on chain-B when it receives a relayer-signed message.
tour.s1: M1 builds the structure graph: release() mints but there is no processed[...] node — no replay protection.
tour.s2: M2 matches against class prototypes; 1-shot is confusable, 5-shot is clearer → “message verification error”.
tour.s3: M3: 5 parties train together without sharing code; DP-SGD clips gradients and adds noise, ε grows to 1.
tour.s4: M4 emits the audit report: high risk, invariant INV-NONCE as a candidate, plus a suggested fix.
tour.s5: Exploit lab: the attacker locks 100 on chain-A then replays release 3 times → receives 400 wDEMO.
tour.s6: The same attack on SafeBridge: replays revert with “replay: processed”.
tour.s7: The M4 report updates: INV-NONCE is now verified by the Exploit lab.

cd3.name: CrossSentry
cd3.topic: Anomaly detection and adaptive trust assessment in cross-chain communication
cd3.summary: Monitoring a live bridge: two-chain event matching with evidence competence, Dempster–Shafer fusion, actor–corridor risk scores and R0–R5 responses with human approval.
steps: M1 · Events & evidence (ECA)
M2 · DS fusion & CRS
M3 · R0–R5 response & G-surv
cd3.replayEnd: End of the recorded scenario — press Reset or pick another scenario.

kpi.invariant: Supply invariant violated: total minted on B exceeds total locked on A.

m2.noSeries: Run a few ticks to get r(t)

m3.noAuto: R4/R5 never self-execute — they run on-chain only after human approval.
m3.giniHint: 0 = even monitoring · high = concentrated on few actors

modal.title: Human approval required
modal.body: CrossSentry proposes a strong measure. Approving sends a real transaction to MintGateway on chain-B; reject if the evidence is weak (e.g. a validator that only co-signed by chance).

tour.s0: CrossSentry monitors a live bridge: LockVault on chain-A, MintGateway (7 validators, t = 3) on chain-B.
tour.s1: Normal traffic: every Locked is matched with its Minted, evidence leans to N, every actor's CRS stays low.
tour.s2: Switch to slow-burn: validator V7, with a good history, starts co-signing “inflated” mints on corridor A→B.
tour.s3: CRS of (V7, A→B) jumps while other corridors stay low → R4 isolate V7 is proposed; a human approves → blockActor on-chain.
tour.s4: From now on mints proposed by V7 are blocked (not enough valid signatures) — the traditional cumulative score has not even caught up.
tour.s5: Collusion scenario: V4–V6 co-sign mints with no matching lock; total minted exceeds total locked.
tour.s6: Several actors at R4 on one corridor → R5 pause bridge is proposed; approve → pause(), every later mint reverts.
tour.s7: G-surv: compare the optimal Θ with the concentration criterion off (w_g = 0) and on (w_g = 1) — balancing detection and fairness.

scHint.slow_burn: V7, with a good history, starts co-signing inflated mints on A→B.
scHint.collusion: V4–V6 + R3 mint without locks — the supply invariant breaks.
scHint.replay: R3 resubmits an already minted msgId (gateway in loose mode).
scHint.boosting: U5–U6 circulate tiny values to inflate reputation.
scHint.oracle_skew: Oracle O1 reports prices skewed +20–40 % on the oracle corridor.
scHint.flash_drain: U3 suddenly moves very large volumes — no rule fires, only the learning channel sees it.
scHint.liveness: V1, V2 offline — delays spread across all relayers: a systemic incident, nobody is blamed.

world.title: Cross-chain Secure SDLC map
world.hint: Select a phase for details · double-click to open the study

p1.story: Before any code is written, the protocol must be designed so the destination chain trusts cryptographic evidence — not relays — without leaking user data.
threats: One party holding the whole key
contrib: Π_univ framework: public statement separated from secret witness
Predicate ZKP + t-of-n threshold signatures checked on-chain
Selective disclosure, revocation and CP-ABE access control

p2.story: Bridge contracts get a multi-source representation (structure, text, cross-chain operations) so a few-shot core recognises vulnerabilities from very few examples, and parties learn jointly without sharing code.
contrib: Multi-source representation: CPG + tokens + cross-chain operation types
Few-shot detection core (prototypes, attention fusion)
Privacy-preserving DP-SGD federated learning (FedVuln)

p3.story: Detections become an audit report: risk tier, evidence, typed invariants and fixes — then the impact is proven with real attacks on an EVM.
contrib: Audit report with invariants (declared / candidate / verified)
Exploit lab verifies invariants on buggy and fixed versions

p4.story: After deployment CrossSentry matches events across both chains, rates evidence competence (ECA), fuses it with Dempster–Shafer and tracks risk per actor–corridor pair.
contrib: Evidence with competence factors κ_L, κ_P (ECA)
Dempster–Shafer fusion with conflict K
Actor–corridor CRS with decay and jumps
R0–R5 responses with human approval

p5.story: Monitoring parameters are tuned periodically to balance detection, operating cost and how concentrated surveillance is (G-surv), so a small group is not over-policed.
contrib: G-surv: Gini index of monitoring intensity
Objective F(Θ) = w_d·U_det − w_g·G_surv − w_c·C_op

big.label: Big picture
big.title: The thesis in one frame
big.thesis: Cross-chain communication must be secured across the whole lifecycle: design on cryptographic evidence, audit contracts before deployment, and monitor adaptively after deployment.
big.problem: Cross-chain bridges hold very large amounts of assets and have suffered several attacks worth hundreds of millions of USD. Each lifecycle phase has its own kind of weakness, so no single technique is enough.
rq: How can a destination chain accept messages on cryptographic evidence while keeping data private?
How can bridge-contract vulnerabilities be detected when labelled data is scarce and code cannot be shared?
How can anomalies be detected and answered in a controlled, fair way while the bridge is running?
big.lifecycle: Life of a cross-chain message — threats & defending studies (hover a study to filter)

cd1.problem: Cross-chain verification often relies on relay reputation and leaks data when proving business predicates.
contrib: Three-layer Π_univ: arithmetic foundation → privacy logic → federated verification
ZKP (Groth16) predicates with statement/witness separation
t-of-n TSS committee verified on the destination chain, nonce against replay
CP-ABE attribute-based access control

cd2.problem: Bridge-contract vulnerabilities are diverse, labelled data is scarce and parties will not share source code.
contrib: CrossGuard M1–M4 pipeline for pre-deployment auditing
Multi-source representation + few-shot core (unitary encoder, Neural ODE, attention)
FedVuln: DP-SGD federated learning + RDP + DAA aggregation
Audit report with typed protocol invariants

cd3.problem: Operational attacks are gradual or coordinated; cumulative reputation reacts slowly and monitoring easily becomes biased.
contrib: CrossSentry: competence-aware evidence (ECA) from both chains
Dempster–Shafer fusion + actor–corridor CRS
R0–R5 responses, R4/R5 require human approval
G-surv: optimisation aware of surveillance concentration

inc.title: Notable cross-chain bridge incidents
inc.body: The largest bridge attacks of recent years. Pick an incident to see, step by step, what the attacker did — and, side by side, what would happen if the bridge were equipped with the thesis tools.

lesson.cd1: Several of the largest losses came from compromised validator/MPC keys or forged proofs: accepting on cryptographic evidence with a distributed threshold removes single points of failure.
lesson.cd2: Message-verification bugs, faulty initialisation and missing access control can be caught before deployment by invariant-driven auditing.
lesson.cd3: Abnormal outflows often ran for hours before anyone noticed: two-chain monitoring with approved responses shortens the damage window.

inc.source: Estimated losses, compiled from public post-mortems by the projects and security analysis firms.

poly.cause: A crafted cross-chain call replaced the "keeper" of the manager contract — the attacker granted itself withdrawal rights.
poly.defense: CĐ2: access-control invariant (INV-ACL) on admin functions; CĐ3: abnormal withdrawals flagged and paused with approval.

qubit.cause: Deposit logic bug: a zero token address was still credited, allowing unbacked mints.
qubit.defense: CĐ2: bridge-logic bug classified by M2, supply invariant (INV-SUPPLY) from M4.

wormhole.cause: Guardian signature verification was bypassed, allowing a forged mint message.
wormhole.defense: CĐ1: the destination chain itself checks t-of-n signatures with ecrecover; CĐ2: missing message verification detected.

ronin.cause: 5 of 9 validator keys were compromised (4 held by one entity), enough to sign withdrawals.
ronin.defense: CĐ1: distributed threshold committee, nobody holds the whole key; CĐ3: CRS + R5 pause when the supply invariant breaks.

harmony.cause: A 2-of-5 multisig; two leaked keys were enough to move assets.
harmony.defense: CĐ1: sound threshold + duplicate-signer rejection; CĐ3: colluding validators detected (Collusion scenario).

nomad.cause: A faulty initialisation made every message count as valid; hundreds of addresses copied the attack transaction.
nomad.defense: CĐ2: message-verification invariants (INV-NONCE/INV-DOMAIN); CĐ3: waves of mints without locks are flagged.

bnb.cause: A forged Merkle (IAVL) proof minted a large amount of new tokens.
bnb.defense: CĐ1: Merkle proof verification + binding commitments to the leaf; CĐ3: mints without matching locks detected.

multichain.cause: MPC keys were centralised with one party; assets were moved out abnormally.
multichain.defense: CĐ1: genuinely distributed TSS; CĐ3: sudden outflows trigger R4/R5.

orbit.cause: 7 of 10 multisig keys were compromised and the vault was drained.
orbit.defense: CĐ1: threshold and key distribution; CĐ3: abnormal withdrawal monitoring with approved pause.

player.title: How the attack unfolds
player.prevented: This step cannot happen — the attack was stopped at step {n} and the assets are still safe in the vault.

steps: The attackers send a fake job offer with a malware-laden PDF to an engineer at the operator. From the infected machine they obtain 4 of the 9 validator keys — all 4 held by the same organization.
5 of 9 signatures are needed to withdraw. The 5th comes from a partner organization that had let the operator "sign on its behalf" months earlier and never revoked it.
With 5 signatures, the attackers craft two formally valid withdrawal orders for the bridge contract.
The contract sees enough signatures and releases 173,600 ETH and 25.5M USDC from the vault to the attackers.
No monitoring raises an alarm. The breach is discovered only 6 days later, when a user cannot withdraw 5,000 ETH.
ronin.block: CĐ1: every signature must be bound to an independent committee member; delegated "sign on behalf" rights and keys of the same entity are not double-counted. The 5th signature is rejected — 4/9 misses the threshold, so the withdrawal is never valid.

outcome.real: ≈ $624M drained and detected 6 days late — the largest bridge hack on record.
outcome.with: The attackers still get 4 keys but miss the threshold; no withdrawal is accepted. CĐ3 would also raise an alarm the moment the vault drains abnormally.

steps: On Solana, the bridge's signature check reads its result from a "system account" supplied by the caller without checking it is the real one. The attacker supplies a fake account pre-filled with "signatures verified".
The bridge trusts the fake account and accepts a mint message never signed by the 19 guardians.
120,000 wETH is minted on Solana — with no matching ETH locked on Ethereum.
The attacker bridges about 93,750 ETH back to Ethereum, draining the bridge's collateral vault.
wormhole.block: CĐ1: the destination contract recovers every signature itself (ecrecover) and counts t-of-n committee members, never trusting a "verified" flag passed in from outside. No real signatures → the message is rejected and nothing is minted.

outcome.real: ≈ $326M; Solana tokens were unbacked until an investor replaced the 120,000 ETH.
outcome.with: The forged message is rejected on arrival. CĐ2 would also flag the "missing message verification" bug before deployment.

steps: A contract upgrade is initialized incorrectly: the value 0x00 is marked as a "trusted Merkle root". Since every unproven message has root 0x00 by default, every message now counts as valid.
The attacker writes a withdrawal message that was never sent from the source chain — the contract accepts it.
100 WBTC leaves the vault in the very first transaction.
The attack transaction is public: hundreds of addresses simply copy it, swap in their own recipient, and jointly empty the vault.
nomad.block: CĐ2: before the upgrade ships, M4 checks the message-verification invariant — "an unproven message is never processed". A trusted 0x00 root violates it, so the upgrade is stopped at the audit gate.

outcome.real: ≈ $190M drained by hundreds of addresses within hours — a "crowd heist".
outcome.with: The faulty upgrade never reaches the chain; there is nothing to exploit or copy.

steps: The cross-chain manager lets a message call any function by name. The attacker searches for a function name whose 4-byte identifier collides with the "change keeper" function — the one that decides who may sign withdrawals.
The message executes: the manager (which holds top privileges) calls the change-keeper function on itself and replaces the keeper key with the attacker's.
Now the "legitimate" keeper, the attacker signs withdrawals and the bridge accepts them.
Assets on three chains (Ethereum, BSC, Polygon) are drained to the attacker.
poly.block: CĐ2: the access-control invariant INV-ACL requires the change-keeper function to be called only through multisig governance, never from the arbitrary message path. M1 flags "arbitrary call into a privileged contract" — the hole is fixed before deployment.

outcome.real: ≈ $611M drained across three chains (most later returned by the attacker).
outcome.with: The change-keeper message is rejected for lacking privilege; the keeper stays, and no forged withdrawal is valid.

steps: The attacker calls the bridge's ETH deposit function without sending any coins. The ETH path uses an empty token address (0x0).
The "transfer token" call to the empty address does not fail — the contract believes it was paid and emits a successful deposit event.
The destination chain sees the deposit and mints qXETH for the attacker — completely unbacked.
The qXETH is posted as collateral to borrow and drain the protocol's real assets.
qubit.block: CĐ2: M2 classifies the bug as "bridge logic" and M4 derives the supply invariant INV-SUPPLY: minted tokens never exceed assets actually locked. A zero deposit does not increase the balance, so nothing is credited.

outcome.real: ≈ $80M borrowed out against collateral that did not exist.
outcome.with: The empty deposit is not credited, no qXETH is minted — the protocol is unaffected.

steps: The bridge uses a 2-of-5 multisig. The attackers obtain 2 keys — exactly the threshold.
With 2 signatures, they sign 11 transactions moving assets out of the bridge.
About $100M (ETH, USDC, WBTC…) is drained and quickly laundered through a mixer.
harmony.block: CĐ1: the committee threshold follows a safe ratio (e.g. 4/5) over independent members. The attackers still obtain 2 keys, but 2/5 is below the threshold, so no transaction can be signed.

outcome.with: Two leaked keys are not enough; the vault stays intact and keys can be rotated. CĐ3 can also detect collusion if signers behave abnormally.

steps: The attacker exploits a bug in the Merkle (IAVL tree) proof checker to build a fake proof for a packet that never existed.
The bridge contract checks the fake proof and deems it valid.
2 million new BNB are minted in two transactions — with no backing.
The attacker rushes over $100M to other chains before the network is halted.
bnb.block: CĐ1: the Merkle proof is fully re-verified and bound to the leaf content (leaf binding) and the chain context against the anchored root. A fake proof does not match the commitment → no mint.

outcome.real: ≈ $570M minted illegitimately; the whole network had to halt.
outcome.with: The fake proof is rejected; no new tokens. CĐ3 would also catch a "mint without matching lock" if one slipped through.

steps: All of the bridge's MPC key shares are controlled by a single person/infrastructure — "distributed" only on paper.
Once the key holder loses control, vault assets move out abnormally across several bridges at once.
The outflow is not stopped; the assets are unrecoverable and the project shuts down.
multichain.block: CĐ1: threshold key shares are assigned to independent members, each holding only one share. Compromising one party yields a single share — not enough to sign a transfer.

outcome.with: Losing one party does not lose the bridge: below threshold, assets stay safe. CĐ3 would trigger R4/R5 on an abnormal outflow.

steps: 7 of the 10 multisig keys are compromised — exactly the 7/10 threshold.
The attackers sign withdrawals that are valid as far as signatures go.
The first withdrawal moves part of the USDT out of the vault.
The following withdrawals take the USDC, ETH, WBTC and DAI — about $81M in total.
orbit.block: CĐ3: the first withdrawal is far outside the bridge's normal profile. Event detection + Dempster–Shafer fusion push the CRS risk score over the threshold → response R5 pauses the bridge (with approval) before the remaining withdrawals.

outcome.real: ≈ $81M drained in a series of withdrawals.
outcome.with: Only the first withdrawal gets through (≈ 15%); the bridge is paused and most assets are kept.
